headline: Forecasters kept a quiet midweek but steadily firmed up a stormy pattern for next week.
summary:
On Sunday, forecasters saw a big dip in the jet stream (a trough) over the western U.S. A deep low offshore was expected to slide south into California, so most of its energy would miss Washington. That left a drier stretch from Tuesday through Friday, with showers tapering early in the week and only spotty rain south of Seattle on Wednesday. That forecast held. A ridge of high pressure, a dome of settled air, moved in later in the week, and the main change was in the details: foggy mornings, some freezing fog, and highs in the 40s and low 50s. Forecasters were more confident about the dry days than about what came after.

The bigger shift was the weekend and beyond. Early on they only hinted that more active weather would return "next weekend." By Tuesday they were describing a wetter, windier pattern for early next week as the jet stream dipped deeply over the Pacific and aimed storms our way. Through Thursday and Friday, confidence grew in strong winds and high seas on the coast Monday into Tuesday, with possible minor coastal flooding at high tides, and rising odds the Skokomish River reaches flood stage later in the week. The weekend itself looks quiet, with only light rain and mountain snow. What remains uncertain is the timing and strength of each storm, and how strong the winds get.

turning_points.what: The midweek offshore storm was expected to miss Washington, and the wetter weather was pushed back to next weekend.
Forecasters added a wetter, windier pattern for early next week and described the weekend system as weak.
A cutoff low was expected to form offshore for the weekend, and coastal flooding from high tides was first mentioned.
Confidence grew in strong winds and high seas Monday into Tuesday, and the Skokomish River was likely to reach flood stage later next week.
